sections.heading: How to get a prompt in three steps
sections.body:
Use this tool when you know what you want from an AI but the words are not coming out right. You do not need to know prompt writing first.

1. Type your idea in the box. Write it the way you would say it to a friend. Messy is fine.
2. Pick the AI you will use under Writing for: ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini or Any AI.
3. Copy the prompt with one click, then paste it into that AI and send it.

The generator writes the prompt, not the answer. Your idea goes to Google Gemini on Lazur's servers, which turns it into a structured prompt for the AI you picked. You get back only the prompt, ready to paste.

You can start on this page or go straight to your AI: [for ChatGPT](https://prompt-generator.lazur.app/chatgpt), [for Claude](https://prompt-generator.lazur.app/claude) or [for Gemini](https://prompt-generator.lazur.app/gemini).

sections.heading: What a good prompt contains
sections.body:
A prompt that works usually says five things. The generator writes all five into the prompt it gives you:

- **Role:** who the AI should act as, such as an editor, a tutor or a travel planner.
- **Task:** the one job to do, in plain words.
- **Context:** the facts the AI needs, such as who will read the answer and what already happened.
- **Constraints:** the limits, such as length, tone, or what to leave out.
- **Output format:** the shape of the answer, such as a list, a table or an email.

If the first prompt is missing one of these, add it to your idea and generate again. The tool only knows what you type, so a clearer idea gives a clearer prompt.

sections.heading: Write an idea that gives a good prompt
sections.body:
Say what you want the AI to make, who it is for, and what a good result looks like. Add any limit you care about, such as a word count or a format.

**Weak idea:** write something about my bakery.

**Better idea:** I run a small bakery and want an Instagram caption for our new lemon loaf. Keep it under 40 words, friendly, and end with a question. The reader is a neighbor in their 30s.

The second version gives a task, an audience and a format. Those three details do most of the work. If you have a text the AI must use, such as your notes or a product description, paste it into your idea too.

There is no app to install. The tool runs in your browser, so you can use it on the same device where you will paste the prompt.

sections.heading: Where to paste the prompt
sections.body:
The prompt is plain text. Open the AI you chose, paste the prompt into its message box, and send it. Read the first answer against your goal. If it misses, change one part of your idea, such as the audience or the format, and generate again. Changing one thing at a time shows you what made the difference.

If you would rather speak your idea than type it, Lazur on your Mac lets you hold two keys and talk, and it types in whatever app you are in. Windows is coming.

sections.heading: How to write a prompt for Claude
sections.body:
Start with the prompt generator for Claude. It writes a prompt for Claude, not an answer, so the last step is yours.

A new chat matters. Older messages in a chat can pull the answer off track, so start fresh each time you try a new prompt.

sections.heading: What Anthropic's guide says about Claude prompts
sections.body:
Anthropic's prompting guide for Claude covers clarity, examples, XML structuring, role prompting and thinking. For everyday tasks, the parts that matter most are a clear task, the context Claude needs, and the output format you want.

The guide also says XML tags help Claude parse complex prompts unambiguously when a prompt mixes instructions, context, examples and inputs. This generator gives you the parts in plain text. If your task has several separate pieces, such as a document to review and a list of rules to follow, wrap each piece in its own tag before you send it.

The guide is the reference to check when a prompt grows large. A short prompt with a clear task usually does better than a long one with many rules.

sections.heading: Tips for a Claude prompt that works
sections.body:
Say what the answer is for. A summary for a busy manager needs different detail from notes for a student, and Claude can only guess if you do not say.

Name the format. Bullet points, a table, a short email and a numbered plan each produce a different answer. If you want a shape that is unusual, add one short example of it to your idea.

Set the limits. Tell Claude the length, the tone and anything to leave out. A limit such as 'no more than 150 words' is easier to follow than 'keep it short'.

Check the reason behind each rule. If you add a rule, add the reason too. Claude follows a rule better when it knows what the rule protects.

sections.heading: When Claude's answer misses
sections.body:
Look at the answer and ask which part of the prompt was weak: the task, the context or the format. Most misses come from one of those three.

Change that part in your idea and generate a new prompt. Then paste it into a fresh Claude chat and compare the two answers. This shows you what your change did, so you learn which words work for you.

Do not add ten new rules at once. When you change many things, you cannot tell which change helped.

sections.heading: How to write a prompt for Gemini
sections.body:
This generator is built on Google Gemini, and it writes a prompt you can take to Gemini or any other AI. It does not answer your task for you.

1. Type your idea into the [Gemini prompt generator](https://prompt-generator.lazur.app/gemini). Include the goal and the reader.
2. Keep Gemini selected under Writing for.
3. Copy the prompt with one click.
4. Paste it into Gemini and send it.

If the first answer is too general, your idea was probably too general. Add one specific detail, such as a number, a deadline or an example of the tone you want, and generate again.

sections.heading: What Google's guide says about Gemini prompts
sections.body:
Google's prompting guide for Gemini starts with clarity. State the task directly, add the constraints, and say how the answer should look, such as a list, a table or a paragraph. Vague requests get vague answers.

The guide also recommends a few varied examples of the answer you want, since one example can make the model copy it too closely. It asks you to provide the background context Gemini needs, so it answers from your facts rather than generic knowledge.

For long inputs, Google suggests putting the context first and the question at the end. Its guide also says to split many instructions into separate steps when one prompt is doing too much. The prompt this tool writes follows the same order: role, task, context, constraints and format.

sections.heading: Use the prompt well in Gemini
sections.body:
Paste the whole prompt, not only the task line. The role, the context and the format are what keep the answer on target.

If the task is large, ask for it in stages. Generate one prompt for the outline, check the result, then generate another for the full draft. Each step gives you a chance to correct the direction before Gemini writes more.

If the answer is wrong, change one part of your idea and generate again. Google's guide calls this iterating: rephrase, reorder, or try the same task in a different format. Keep the version that gives you the answer you need.

sections.heading: Why a written prompt helps
sections.body:
A rough request leaves the AI to guess the role, the reader and the format. A structured prompt answers those questions up front, so the AI spends its effort on the work.

You can see the difference in one run. Write a request the way you would type it into a search box, then generate a prompt from the same idea and compare the two answers. The one with a role, a reader and a format is usually the one you can use.

If you would rather speak your idea than type it, Lazur on your Mac lets you hold two keys and talk, and it types in whatever app you are in. Windows is coming.

faq.q: How do I create a prompt for Gemini AI?
faq.a: Be specific about the task, add the background Gemini needs, and state the output format and any length limit. For long input, put the context first and the question last. This generator writes that structure for you: type your idea, pick Gemini under Writing for, and copy the result.

faq.q: What are the best prompts for Gemini AI?
faq.a: There is no single best prompt, because it depends on the task. Good prompts are specific, give the context Gemini needs, and say how the answer should look. Start from your own goal with the generator, then change one part at a time to see what Gemini does with it.

sections.heading: What OpenAI's guide says about ChatGPT prompts
sections.body:
OpenAI's prompt engineering guide asks you to be explicit. Spell out the logic and the data the task needs. Its guide says models work best with precise instructions, and it lists a clear output format as one of the strategies that change results.

The guide also recommends examples of the input and output you want, plus any reference text the model must use. Give it that text, not a summary of it, when accuracy matters.

OpenAI also suggests structuring the prompt with headers, lists or XML tags, and placing the context near the end. The prompt this tool writes follows the same order, so you can read each part and change the one that is off.

sections.heading: Paste reference text when you have it
sections.body:
Some tasks depend on a text: your notes, a product page, a contract clause or a draft. ChatGPT answers better when it can see that text, so add it after you copy the prompt, and place it near the end.

Label the text in the prompt, for example 'Notes:' followed by the text. A clear label tells ChatGPT which part is the source and which part is the instruction.

If the text is long, keep the task short. Ask for one thing at a time, such as a summary or a list of questions, rather than a rewrite of everything.

sections.heading: When the answer is not what you wanted
sections.body:
Read the answer and find the part that missed: the role, the reader, the format or the limits. Change that part in your idea and generate a new prompt.

Paste the new prompt into a fresh ChatGPT chat. Older messages can steer the answer, so a new chat gives you a fair comparison.

Keep a prompt that works. Copy it into a note with the task it solved, so you can reuse it next time.
